newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Bonn under pressure on EU jobs plan.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bonn under pressure on EU jobs plan.

text.p: The German government came under increasing pressure on Wednesday to withdraw its resistance to a chapter on employment creation that is being prepared for possible inclusion in new European Union treaty reforms.
Oskar Lafontaine, chief of the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), said Bonn's continued opposition to the initiative threatened Europe's long-term stability.
"Europe must be a Europe in which its citizens have access to employment," Lafontaine said in a parliamentary speech.

Details of the proposed new chapter are unclear. But the SPD and newly-elected French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin had directly before the left-wing victory in France launched a plan that would coordinate employment policy across the continent.

German Foreign Ministry State Secretary Werner Hoyer met European foreign ministers in Luxembourg on Tuesday, with one of the aims of the talks being to allay German fears about the cost of an EU-wide jobs initiative.

Hoyer said there had been some progress in the talks but that a "range of difficult points remained open". EU heads of state are due to meet in Amsterdam on June 16 to discuss EU treaty reforms, including on employment.
Dieter Schulte, Germany's top trade union official, attacked Hoyer for hard-headedly defending an increasingly isolated position.

"Hoyer is probably trying with this stubbornness to extract a few negotiating advantages in the run-up to the Amsterdam summit," Schulte, chairman of the German Trade Union Federation (DGB), said in a statement.
"All the other countries have however grasped that people need the type of signal on Europe that a serious chapter on jobs...could offer," he added.
The new British government earlier announced a three-point plan to reduce unemployment on the continent, currently put at 18 million, that it will present to EU finance ministers next Monday.
The scheme involves among other things the setting up of a task force to help small and medium-sized firms create jobs, and a continued push for a completely free European internal trading market.

Lafontaine of the Geman SPD's had earlier said that job creation policies should be anchored "right at centre" of the push towards monetary union, which so far had concentrated more on assuring the convergence of other economic criteria.
He further cited the expansion of European transport networks, a much-favoured project of the European left, as one clear opportunity to create lasting and valuable employment across the continent.
